name: Dusty Rose
lede: Dusty Rose is a muted pink-red close to the color of a garnet, carried in the ISCC-NBS 1955 dictionary and, almost a century and a half earlier, in Werner's 1821 nomenclature.

sections.title: From a mineral to a modern pink
sections.body:
Werner's 1821 nomenclature of colors, the system Charles Darwin carried on his travels, lists this point as its color number 93 among the reds, matched to Precious Garnet; Werner's plates are an aged, hand-colored swatch book, so the reading is approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS 1955 dictionary separately places it in block 251, among colors it calls "dark purplish pink", 4.5 units away [2]. The 2010 xkcd survey records the everyday name "dusty rose" again, well over a century after Werner [3].

In Munsell terms it reads about 1.6R 5.6/7.1 [2]. Our library's nearest named neighbor is [[dirty-pink]], and a near-duplicate under Werner's own system is Crimson Red, only 2.2 units away [2][3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this color in 23 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.1 percent, as photographed [4]. The earliest dated match is an anonymous *Bishop Saint with a Donor*, from about 1400, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [4]. It turns up across widely different traditions, from Diego Velázquez's 1650 *[[painting:commons-Q118895689|Pope Innocent X]]* to Mughal and Rajput court paintings, where it appears at more than ten times the archive's overall rate [4]. Across its matches it plays a mid-tone over half the time, a highlight close to a third of the time, and rarely a shadow [4]. These counts are computed color matches on photographs of aged, varnished paintings, not pigment identifications [4].
